claims.source: In control neurons, RhoA activation correlated strikingly with individual dendrite behavior (Figure 3e,g,h): extending dendrites showed low levels of RhoA activation, while retracting dendrites had high levels thereof.
claims.evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3e,g,h.

claims.claim: These differences in RhoA activation were persistent throughout the time course and especially pronounced at the dendrite tips.
claims.source: These differences in RhoA activation were persistent throughout the time course and especially pronounced at the dendrite tips (Figure 3g, left), though also apparent at branch points (Figure 3h, left).
claims.evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3g,h.

claims.claim: BAI1 Kd profoundly affected the relationship between RhoA activation and dendrite behavior.
claims.source: BAI1 Kd profoundly affected these phenomena. BAI1 Kd neurons had lower RhoA activation levels throughout the time course (Figure 3f–h, right).
claims.evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3f-h.

claims.claim: At dendrite tips, there was no difference in RhoA activation between extending and retracting dendrites in BAI1 Kd neurons.
claims.source: At dendrite tips, which were the best indicators of dendrite behavior in control neurons, there was no difference in RhoA activation between extending and retracting dendrites in BAI Kd neurons (Figure 3f,g).
claims.evidence: Supported by longitudinal FRET data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claims.claim: RhoA activation levels at dendrite tips strongly and negatively correlated with dendrite growth in control neurons.
claims.source: The best match was shown in Figure 3i, wherein RhoA activation levels at dendrite tips strongly and negatively correlated with dendrite growth.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claims.claim: BAI1 Kd completely eliminated the correlation between RhoA activation at dendrite tips and dendrite growth.
claims.source: BAI1 Kd, however, completely eliminated this correlation (Figure 3i).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claims.claim: RhoA activation at dendritic tips is the primary driver of dendritic retraction in wild type neurons.
claims.source: These data suggest that RhoA activation at dendritic tips is the primary driver of dendritic retraction in wild type neurons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the strong negative correlation between RhoA activation at tips and dendrite growth (Figure 3i).

claims.claim: Narciclasine activates RhoA in neurons.
claims.source: We first confirmed that narciclasine activated RhoA in neurons by treating Raichu-RhoA-expressing hippocampal neurons with vehicle or 10 nM narciclasine. Narciclasine-treated neurons exhibited increased RhoA activation throughout the dendritic arbor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claims.claim: Low dose narciclasine had no effect on the morphology of control neurons assayed on 21 DIV, but prevented BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth.
claims.source: We therefore applied narciclasine to 17 DIV neurons and found that this low dose of narciclasine had no effect on the morphology of control neurons assayed on 21 DIV, but prevented BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth with respect to dendrite length (Figure 4a,b), dendrite number (Figure 4a,c), branch points (Figure 4a,d), and Sholl curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 4a-d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d.

claims.claim: Narciclasine had no effect on primary dendrite number.
claims.source: Like BAI1 Kd, narciclasine had no effect on primary dendrite number (Figure 4a,e).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a,e.

claims.claim: BAI1 Kd caused decreases in spine density.
claims.source: As we have previously reported, BAI1 Kd caused decreases in spine density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b) and maximum diameter (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,e), but increases in filopod density (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,c) and spine length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,d).
claims.evidence: Supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claims.claim: Narciclasine did not rescue the spine density defects caused by BAI1 Kd.
claims.source: Unlike dendritic arbor morphology, narciclasine did not rescue the spine density defects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b), though it did block increases in spine length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,d) and decreased spine maximum diameter by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,e), consistent with known effects of RhoA on spine morphology (Tolias et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by spine morphology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claims.claim: Y-27632 rescued dendritic arbors from the contraction caused by BAI1 OX.
claims.source: As above, BAI1 OX led to lower total dendrite length (Figure 4f,g), fewer dendrites (Figure 4f,h), fewer branch points (Figure 4f,i), and contracted Sholl curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f,g). All of these effects were prevented by Y-27632 (Figure 4f–i, Figure 4—figure supplement 1f–g).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 4f-i and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-g.

claims.claim: Y-27632 did not affect the number of primary dendrites.
claims.source: Y-27632 did not affect the number of primary dendrites (Figure 4f,j).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4f,j.

claims.claim: Modulating RhoA signaling with narciclasine or Y-27632 rescues dendritic arbors from the effects of altered BAI1 signals.
claims.source: Thus, modulating RhoA signaling with narciclasine (RhoA activation) or Y-27632 (ROCK inhibition) rescues dendritic arbors from the effects of altered BAI1 signals, suggesting a role for RhoA signaling downstream of BAI1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments with narciclasine and Y-27632 (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Deletion or mutation of the TEV motif, helical domain, GPCR domain, and proline-rich region resulted in well-expressed mutants that are surface-localized and capable of rescuing BAI1 Kd-induced increases in dendrite length, number, and branches as effectively as wild-type BAI1.
claims.source: Deletion or mutation of each of these domains resulted in well-expressed mutants that are surface-localized (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b and Tu et al., 2018) and capable of rescuing BAI1 Kd-induced increases in dendrite length, number, and branches as effectively as wild-type BAI1 (Figure 5a–c,f–h).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5a-c,f-h and surface localization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b.

claims.claim: The ∆TEV BAI1 mutant rescued arbor growth arrest but does not rescue spine development.
claims.source: It is especially interesting that the ∆TEV BAI1 mutant rescued arbor growth arrest, as it does not rescue spine development (Duman et al., 2013), arguing against BAI1's effect on arbors arising as a secondary effect from its effects on synaptogenesis.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing ∆TEV rescues dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5a,f-h) and citation to previous work showing it does not rescue spine development.

claims.claim: Suppression of activity did not cause arbor overgrowth in control hippocampal neurons, nor did increasing activity prevent overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons.
claims.source: To further address this point, we demonstrated that suppression of activity did not cause arbor overgrowth in control hippocampal neurons, nor did increasing activity prevent overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1h,i).
claims.evidence: Supported by data from activity manipulation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1h,i.

claims.claim: Deletion of the proline-rich region rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth.
claims.source: We also deleted a proline-rich region that links BAI1 to the scaffold IRSp53 (Oda et al., 1999), and found that this mutant also rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5d,f–h).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5d,f-h.

claims.claim: Neither BAI1 Kd nor any of the mutants affected primary dendrite number.
claims.source: Neither BAI1 Kd nor any of the mutants affected primary dendrite number (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), and all mutants were expressed at levels comparable to wild-type BAI1 (Figure 5a–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c–f).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: No previously reported BAI1 signaling modality is necessary for restricting dendrite growth.
claims.source: In sum, no previously reported BAI1 signaling modality is necessary for restricting dendrite growth.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing that deletion of known signaling domains does not prevent rescue of dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5).

claims.claim: BAI1-∆N-term. did not rescue dendritic overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons.
claims.source: However, unlike the other mutants, it did not rescue dendritic overgrowth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 5e,f–h).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5e,f-h.

claims.claim: Extracellular ligand binding is likely required for BAI1-mediated arbor growth arrest.
claims.source: Thus, extracellular ligand binding is likely required for BAI1-mediated arbor growth arrest.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the failure of the ∆N-term mutant to rescue dendrite overgrowth (Figure 5e,f-h).

claims.claim: All of the BAI1 mutants that rescued dendrite overgrowth also rescued RhoA activation, while BAI1-∆N-term. failed to rescue both defects.
claims.source: Further, all of the BAI1 mutants that rescued dendrite overgrowth (∆TEV, RKR, ∆GPCR, and ∆PRR) also rescued RhoA activation, while BAI1-∆N-term. failed to rescue both defects (Figure 6a,b).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 6a,b.

claims.claim: BAI1 functions through RhoA to mediate dendritic arbor growth arrest.
claims.source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that BAI1 functions through RhoA to mediate dendritic arbor growth arrest.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the correlation between rescue of dendrite overgrowth and rescue of RhoA activation (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Little or no interaction was detected between BAI1 and Bcr before DIV 17, but the interaction was readily detected at the time of dendritic growth arrest.
claims.source: Interestingly, we detected little or no interaction between BAI1 and Bcr before DIV 17, but the interaction was readily detected at the time of dendritic growth arrest (Figure 7a–c).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a-c.

claims.claim: No interaction was detected between BAI1 and Abr.
claims.source: No interaction was detected between BAI1 and Abr (Figure 7a,b).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claims.claim: Bcr overexpression balanced BAI1 Kd, giving rise to arbors of normal length and complexity while Abr OX did not.
claims.source: However, Bcr OX balanced BAI1 Kd, giving rise to arbors of normal length and complexity while Abr OX did not (Figure 7d–f).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 7d-f.

claims.claim: The effectiveness of Bcr in causing arbor contraction was blunted by BAI1 loss.
claims.source: Moreover, the effectiveness of Bcr in causing arbor contraction, assayed by the final arbor length as a function of Bcr OX level, was blunted by BAI1 loss (Figure 7g–i).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7g-i.

claims.claim: BAI1 activates Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in neurons.
claims.source: This supports the idea that BAI1 activates Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in neurons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the functional interaction data showing Bcr rescues BAI1 Kd and BAI1 loss blunts Bcr effectiveness (Figure 7d-i).

claims.claim: No functional interaction with Abr was detected.
claims.source: No such functional interaction with Abr was detected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1d,e).
claims.evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1d,e.

claims.claim: Both the biochemical and functional data support a role for Bcr in BAI1 signaling rather than Abr.
claims.source: Thus, both the biochemical and functional data support a role for Bcr in BAI1 signaling rather than Abr.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined biochemical and functional data showing BAI1-Bcr interaction and functional rescue (Figure 7).

claims.claim: Bcr activates RhoA in Cos-7 cells.
claims.source: We detected RhoA activation in response to Bcr expression in Cos-7 cells (Figure 7j,k).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in Cos-7 cells shown in Figure 7j,k.

claims.claim: Co-expression with BAI1 greatly enhanced Bcr RhoA-GEF activity.
claims.source: Moreover, co-expression with BAI1 greatly enhanced Bcr RhoA-GEF activity (Figure 7j,k), despite comparable expression of the proteins in the cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1f), suggesting that BAI1 stimulates this activity.
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET measurements in Cos-7 cells shown in Figure 7j,k.

claims.claim: Bcr loss caused dendritic overgrowth that was rescued by expression of wild type Bcr.
claims.source: As previously reported (Park et al., 2012), Bcr loss caused dendritic overgrowth that was rescued by expression of wild type Bcr (Figure 8a–c).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data from Bcr KO neurons shown in Figure 8a-c.

claims.claim: When the rescue was attempted using mutants of Bcr deficient for either Rac1-GAP or RhoA-GEF activity, neither dendritic length nor dendrite number was rescued.
claims.source: Strikingly, when the rescue was attempted using mutants of Bcr deficient for either Rac1-GAP (as previously reported [Park et al., 2012]) or RhoA-GEF activity, neither dendritic length (Figure 8b) nor dendrite number (Figure 8c) was rescued.
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data from Bcr KO neurons expressing mutant Bcr shown in Figure 8b,c.

claims.claim: Overexpression of neither Bcr-GAP-dead nor Bcr-GEF-dead mutant rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth in rat hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Overexpression of neither mutant rescued BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth in rat hippocampal neurons assayed by length (Figure 8d,e) or dendrite number (Figure 8d,f).
claims.evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 8d-f.

claims.claim: BAI1-orchestrated dendrite growth arrest requires RhoA activation by Bcr downstream of BAI1 in concert with the Rac1-GAP activity of Bcr.
claims.source: These results suggest that BAI1-orchestrated dendrite growth arrest requires RhoA activation by Bcr downstream of BAI1 in concert with the Rac1-GAP activity of Bcr.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both GAP and GEF activities of Bcr for rescue (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Dendrite growth arrest requires a great change in the signaling environment within dendrites akin to a state change.
claims.source: This suggests that dendrite growth arrest requires a great change in the signaling environment within dendrites akin to a state change.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both RhoA activation and Rac1 inhibition by Bcr (Figure 8).

claims.claim: BAI1 is enriched in hippocampal dendritic spines.
claims.source: We previously demonstrated that BAI1 is enriched in hippocampal dendritic spines (Duman et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: BAI1 was present at branch points at 14, 17, and 21 DIV, but did not vary relative to total dendritic BAI1 staining over this time course.
claims.source: BAI1 was present at branch points at 14, 17, and 21 DIV, but did not vary relative to total dendritic BAI1 staining over this time course (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f.

claims.claim: 14 DIV neurons exhibited little BAI1 staining at the dendritic tips, but clear BAI1 staining appeared by 17 DIV and persisted through at least 21 DIV.
claims.source: 14 DIV neurons exhibited little BAI1 staining at the dendritic tips, but clear BAI1 staining appeared by 17 DIV and persisted through at least 21 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f.

claims.claim: BAI1 is present throughout dendrites and critical growth loci at the time of dendrite growth arrest.
claims.source: Thus, BAI1 is present throughout dendrites and critical growth loci at the time of dendrite growth arrest.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the localization data showing BAI1 at tips and branch points at 17 DIV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f).

claims.claim: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth.
claims.source: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999), but the dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood (see below).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on RhoA function.

claims.claim: The dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood.
claims.source: RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999), but the dynamics of RhoA activation throughout dendritic development are not well understood (see below).
claims.evidence: Supported by the lack of comprehensive understanding in the literature.

claims.claim: BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips.
claims.source: Moreover, BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips, which seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
claims.evidence: Supported by FRET data showing lower RhoA activation and loss of correlation with dendrite growth in BAI1 Kd neurons (Figure 3).

claims.claim: RhoA activation at the tips seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
claims.source: Moreover, BAI1 loss globally suppresses RhoA activity and uncouples dendritic growth from RhoA activation at the tips, which seems to drive dendritic behavior late in development.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the strong correlation between RhoA activation at tips and dendrite growth in control neurons (Figure 3i).

claims.claim: Bcr-dependent activation of RhoA is not sufficient to cause growth arrest but also requires Bcr-mediated inhibition of Rac1.
claims.source: This Bcr-dependent activation of RhoA, however is not sufficient to cause growth arrest but also requires Bcr-mediated inhibition of the complementary small GTPase Rac1.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing that both GAP-dead and GEF-dead Bcr mutants fail to rescue dendrite overgrowth (Figure 8).

claims.claim: These results strongly implicate a BAI1-Bcr-RhoA pathway in regulating dendritic volume in the hippocampus.
claims.source: These results strongly implicate a BAI1-Bcr-RhoA pathway in regulating dendritic volume in the hippocampus, which is intriguing, especially given the links between BAI1 and ASD (Michaelson et al., 2012; Chahrour et al., 2008; Urdinguio et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing BAI1 activates RhoA through Bcr to restrict dendrite growth.

claims.claim: BAI1 Kd leads to a loss of dendritic spines and synapses in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: We previously reported that BAI1 Kd also causes a marked decrease in spine density in both cultured hippocampal neurons and in vivo in CA1 and cortical pyramidal neurons (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018). That BAI1 Kd leads to a loss of dendritic spines and synapses in hippocampal neurons (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018) could be misconstrued as the explanation for the longer arbors reported here.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The effect of BAI1 on dendritic arbors is not a side effect of synapse loss.
claims.source: Thus, we can affirm that the effect of BAI1 on dendritic arbors is not a side effect of synapse loss.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing ∆TEV rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits, and narciclasine rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits (Figures 4-5).

claims.claim: BAI1's role in restricting arbor growth is independent of its effect on promoting dendritic spinogenesis/synaptogenesis, and is mediated by the activation of RhoA by Bcr.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that BAI1's role in restricting arbor growth is independent of its effect on promoting dendritic spinogenesis/synaptogenesis, and is mediated by the activation of RhoA by Bcr.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing independence of arbor and spine effects and the role of RhoA and Bcr.

claims.claim: A recent study characterizing global BAI1 KO mice reported no change in dendritic arbor length or spine density as a result of BAI1 loss.
claims.source: A recent study characterizing global BAI1 KO mice reported no change in dendritic arbor length or spine density as a result of BAI1 loss, though no quantitative dendritic data were presented (Zhu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice.

claims.claim: BAI1 KO mice have decreased hippocampus-based learning, lowered threshold for LTP, LTP in response to LTD-provoking stimuli, and decreased PSD thickness.
claims.source: These animals have diminished hippocampus-based learning, lowered threshold for LTP, LTP in response to LTD-provoking stimuli, and decreased PSD thickness (Zhu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice.

claims.claim: BAI1 KO mice have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95.
claims.source: BAI1 KO mice also have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95, which we also reported in our sparse Kd models (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018), and BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (Zhu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 KO mice and previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2.
claims.source: BAI1 KO mice also have decreased levels of the postsynaptic scaffold PSD95, which we also reported in our sparse Kd models (Duman et al., 2013; Tu et al., 2018), and BAI1 stabilizes PSD95 by binding to and inhibiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (Zhu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on BAI1 function.

claims.claim: BAI1 may assert its effects by conferring an advantage to synapses and/or a disadvantage to dendrites that express it.
claims.source: Further, BAI1 may assert its effects by conferring an advantage to synapses and/or a disadvantage to dendrites that express it. If this were the case, then global loss of BAI1 would even the playing field and the effects of its loss might be greatly ameliorated.
claims.evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain differences between global KO and sparse Kd.

claims.claim: Global NL1 KO is associated with essentially no effect on spine or synapse density, but sparse NL1 removal causes dramatically lower spine and synapse densities.
claims.source: While NL1 plays a crucial role in synaptic function, global NL1 KO is associated with essentially no effect on spine or synapse density (Kwon et al., 2012). However, if NL1 is removed from a sparse population of neurons, these neurons exhibit dramatically lower spine and synapse densities (Kwon et al., 2012); conversely, if NL1 is overexpressed sparsely, these neurons display higher spine densities and larger spines (Dahlhaus et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on NL1.

claims.claim: There is a functional interaction between BAI1 and NL1 in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, we recently demonstrated a functional interaction between BAI1 and NL1 in hippocampal neurons (Tu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to recent work by the authors.

claims.claim: BAI1 confers an advantage to synapses and a disadvantage to dendritic branches that express it during development.
claims.source: Based on these considerations, we submit that BAI1 confers an advantage to synapses and a disadvantage to dendritic branches that express it during development. These effects are apparent when BAI1 is overexpressed or knocked down on a background of neurons normally expressing BAI1 in culture or in vivo, but that global removal of BAI1 removes this competitive advantage/disadvantage and makes the effects of BAI1 much less evident.
claims.evidence: Speculative reasoning based on comparison with NL1 and differences between global KO and sparse manipulations.

claims.claim: Bcr possesses a Rac1-GAP domain and a RhoA-GEF domain.
claims.source: Bcr possesses multiple functional domains, but its most intriguing feature may be that it possesses a Rac1-GAP domain and a RhoA-GEF domain (Park et al., 2012; Rochelle et al., 2013; Tala et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr structure.

claims.claim: Bcr was previously shown to restrict dendrite development and spinogenesis/synaptogenesis through its Rac1-GAP functionality.
claims.source: Bcr was previously shown to restrict dendrite development and spinogenesis/synaptogenesis through its Rac1-GAP functionality (Um et al., 2014; Park et al., 2012), so the requirement for RhoA-GEF activity was unexpected.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr function.

claims.claim: Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has mostly been described in the context of the p210bcr-abl fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome that is associated with virtually all cases of chronic myeloid leukemia.
claims.source: This activity of Bcr has mostly been described in the context of the p210bcr-abl fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome that is associated with virtually all cases of chronic myeloid leukemia, and activates RhoA and various downstream targets thereof (Rochelle et al., 2013; Tala et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bcr-Abl.

claims.claim: A physiological role for Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has been suggested in keratinocyte differentiation.
claims.source: A physiological role for Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity has been suggested in keratinocyte differentiation, though there is no obvious role for its Rac1-GAP activity in this system (Dubash et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Bcr function.

claims.claim: Bcr must both activate an inhibitor of arborization (RhoA) and inhibit an activator of arborization (Rac1) in order to precipitate arbor growth arrest.
claims.source: Our results indicate that Bcr must both activate an inhibitor of arborization (RhoA) and inhibit an activator of arborization (Rac1) in order to precipitate arbor growth arrest (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing requirement for both GAP and GEF activities (Figure 8).

claims.claim: The arrest signal is very high in magnitude, and perhaps requires multiple inputs.
claims.source: This suggests that the arrest signal is very high in magnitude, and perhaps requires multiple inputs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the requirement for both RhoA activation and Rac1 inhibition.

claims.claim: RhoA cycles between a GDP-bound inactive form and a GTP-bound active form.
claims.source: Like all small GTPases, RhoA cycles between a GDP-bound inactive form and a GTP-bound active form (Evers et al., 2000; Ridley, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by established knowledge about small GTPases and citations.

claims.claim: Activated RhoA generally mediates inhibitory/repulsive processes in the nervous system.
claims.source: Activated RhoA generally mediates inhibitory/repulsive processes in the nervous system (Redmond and Ghosh, 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claims.claim: RhoA is widely accepted as a physiological antagonist of dendrite growth in a variety of model systems.
claims.source: While RhoA is widely accepted as a physiological antagonist of dendrite growth in a variety of model systems, the studies on which this notion was built primarily employed dominant negative and constitutively active RhoA mutants (Sin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2000; Nakayama et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000; Ruchhoeft et al., 1999) or studied the process at a much earlier stage (Takano et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on RhoA function.

claims.claim: Overexpression of either type of GTPase mutant has great potential for broad-spectrum effects that cannot definitively be attributed to the target Rho-GTPase.
claims.source: We now know that overexpression of either type of GTPase mutant has great potential for broad-spectrum effects that cannot definitively be attributed to the target Rho-GTPase (Schiller, 2006; Vega and Ridley, 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on GTPase mutants.

claims.claim: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages.
claims.source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claims.claim: RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus.
claims.source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to literature on RhoA function.

claims.claim: RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin.
claims.source: However, more recent studies have verified the core finding that RhoA acts to oppose dendrite growth and expanded the contexts within which this might happen: RhoA activation by Arhgef1 opposes dendrite growth in mouse cortex at very early (>P5) stages (Xiang et al., 2016); RhoA activation by the neuropeptide orphanin FQ opposes developmental BDNF-stimulated dendrite growth in granule cells of the dentate gyrus (Alder et al., 2013); RhoA inhibits the expression of the branch promoter cypin (Chen and Firestein, 2007); failure to inactivate RhoA late in development leads to dendrite loss (Lin et al., 2013); and UVB injury promotes dendrite growth by decreasing RhoA expression (Jian et al., 2014).

results.result: BAI1 loss causes dendritic hypertrophy in hippocampal neurons both in vivo and in culture, while BAI1 overexpression causes dendrite retraction. In vivo knockdown via in utero electroporation at E14 and analysis at P21 showed increased dendrite density, length, number, and branch points in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These effects were reproduced in cultured hippocampal neurons and rescued by reintroduction of RNAi-resistant BAI1.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C45, and C49-C59 are well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches. The in vivo data (Figure 1a-h) using sparse knockdown via in utero electroporation demonstrates increased dendrite density, length, number, and branch points in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These findings are independently replicated in cultured neurons (Figure 1i-k) using two different shRNAs, with rescue by RNAi-resistant BAI1 confirming specificity. The bidirectional effects (loss-of-function causing overgrowth, gain-of-function causing retraction) strengthen the conclusion that BAI1 actively restricts dendritic growth. Quantitative morphological analyses support all claims.

results.result: BAI1-mediated dendritic growth restriction occurs specifically during the late developmental transition from growth to stability (17-21 DIV in culture). Longitudinal imaging revealed that control neurons stop growing at 17 DIV while BAI1 Kd neurons continue growing through 21 DIV. BAI1 overexpression causes dendrite retraction between 17-21 DIV, with decreased branch formation and increased branch elimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46, and C60-C70 are strongly supported by longitudinal imaging data (Figure 2). The temporal specificity is demonstrated by showing that BAI1 Kd neurons are initially shorter than controls at 10 DIV but surpass controls by 17 DIV, with continued growth through 21 DIV while controls stabilize. The complementary BAI1 overexpression experiments showing retraction specifically between 17-21 DIV provide bidirectional support. Branch dynamics data (formations and eliminations) further support the late-acting nature of BAI1's effects. The timing correlates with the developmental transition from growth to stability, as claimed.

results.result: BAI1-mediated dendrite growth arrest is independent of its Rac1-dependent synaptogenic function and does not require any previously known BAI1 signaling domains. The ΔN-terminal mutant (lacking extracellular ligand-binding domains) fails to rescue dendrite overgrowth, suggesting extracellular ligand binding is required. Activity manipulations do not affect BAI1 Kd-induced overgrowth.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C92-C99, C127-C128 are well-supported by systematic domain deletion/mutation experiments (Figure 5). The key finding that the ΔTEV mutant rescues dendrite overgrowth but not spine deficits (C93) demonstrates independence of these two BAI1 functions. Deletions of the TEV motif, helical domain, GPCR domain, and proline-rich region all rescue dendrite overgrowth (C92, C95-C97), indicating these known signaling domains are dispensable. Only the ΔN-terminal mutant fails to rescue (C98-C99), implicating extracellular ligand binding. Activity manipulation experiments (C94) further support independence from synaptic activity. The narciclasine rescue of dendrite but not spine phenotypes (C127) provides additional orthogonal support.

results.result: BAI1 drives late RhoA activation in dendrites coincident with growth arrest. Control neurons show marked increases in RhoA activation at dendrite tips and branch points late in development (17-23 DIV), which is blunted and delayed in BAI1 Kd neurons. RhoA activation at dendrite tips strongly correlates with dendrite behavior in control neurons (extending dendrites have low RhoA, retracting have high RhoA), but this correlation is eliminated in BAI1 Kd neurons. RhoA KO neurons show increased arbor size at 19 DIV.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C71-C83, C122-C123, and C153-C155 are strongly supported by comprehensive FRET-based measurements of RhoA activation (Figure 3). The temporal dynamics showing late RhoA activation peak in control neurons (C71-C72) that is blunted in BAI1 Kd (C73-C74) are well-documented. The correlation analysis (Figure 3i) demonstrating strong negative correlation between RhoA activation at tips and dendrite growth in controls (C81), which is eliminated in BAI1 Kd (C82), is particularly compelling. Longitudinal tracking of individual dendrites (C76-C79) provides additional support. RhoA KO data (C75) provides genetic validation. The claims about RhoA activation levels determining dendrite fate (C155) are supported by persistent differences between extending and retracting dendrites.

results.result: Pharmacological modulation of RhoA signaling rescues BAI1-mediated dendrite phenotypes. Narciclasine (RhoA activator) at 10 nM prevents BAI1 Kd-mediated dendrite overgrowth without affecting control neurons or rescuing spine deficits. Y-27632 (ROCK inhibitor) rescues dendrite retraction caused by BAI1 overexpression. All BAI1 mutants that rescue dendrite overgrowth also rescue RhoA activation, while ΔN-terminal fails to rescue both.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91, C100-C101 are well-supported by pharmacological rescue experiments (Figure 4) and correlation with mutant rescue data (Figure 6). The narciclasine experiments demonstrate RhoA activation in neurons (C84) and selective rescue of dendrite but not spine phenotypes (C85-C88), supporting independence of these functions. Y-27632 rescue of BAI1 overexpression phenotype (C89-C90) provides complementary evidence. The correlation between dendrite rescue and RhoA activation rescue across multiple BAI1 mutants (C100) strongly supports the mechanistic link. However, the pharmacological agents have known off-target effects, which the authors acknowledge but address through use of low concentrations and controls.

results.result: BAI1 associates with Bcr (but not Abr) late in development (≥17 DIV) and stimulates Bcr's cryptic RhoA-GEF activity. Bcr overexpression rescues BAI1 Kd-induced dendrite overgrowth, while Abr does not. BAI1 co-expression enhances Bcr RhoA-GEF activity in Cos-7 cells. The effectiveness of Bcr in causing arbor contraction is blunted by BAI1 loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C102-C110 are well-supported by biochemical and functional data (Figure 7). Immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate temporal specificity of BAI1-Bcr interaction (≥17 DIV) but no BAI1-Abr interaction (C102-C103). Functional rescue experiments show Bcr but not Abr rescues BAI1 Kd phenotype (C104), and BAI1 loss blunts Bcr effectiveness (C105), supporting functional interaction. FRET measurements in Cos-7 cells demonstrate BAI1 enhances Bcr RhoA-GEF activity (C109-C110). The convergence of biochemical interaction, temporal correlation with growth arrest, and functional rescue provides strong support. However, the Cos-7 cell data (C109-C110) is in a heterologous system, which may not fully recapitulate neuronal context.

results.result: Both Bcr's RhoA-GEF activity and Rac1-GAP activity are required for dendrite growth arrest. In Bcr KO neurons, neither GAP-dead nor GEF-dead Bcr mutants rescue dendrite overgrowth. Similarly, neither mutant rescues BAI1 Kd-induced overgrowth in rat neurons. This suggests dendrite growth arrest requires a large signaling change akin to a state change, with simultaneous RhoA activation and Rac1 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C111-C115, C124, C141-C142 are strongly supported by systematic mutant rescue experiments in both Bcr KO and BAI1 Kd backgrounds (Figure 8). The requirement for both GAP and GEF activities is demonstrated by failure of either single mutant to rescue in both genetic contexts (C112-C113). This is a key mechanistic finding showing that simple RhoA activation is insufficient. The interpretation that this represents a 'state change' requiring large signaling shifts (C115, C142) is a reasonable inference from the dual requirement, though this remains somewhat speculative. The convergence of results in two different genetic backgrounds (Bcr KO and BAI1 Kd) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: BAI1 localization changes during development. BAI1 is enriched in dendritic spines and present at branch points throughout 14-21 DIV. At dendrite tips, BAI1 staining is minimal at 14 DIV but appears by 17 DIV and persists through 21 DIV, coinciding with the timing of growth arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-f). The temporal appearance of BAI1 at dendrite tips coinciding with growth arrest timing (C118-C119) provides correlative support for BAI1's role in this transition. However, the localization data is descriptive and correlative rather than mechanistic. The claim about spine enrichment (C116) is supported by citation to previous work. The quantification shows BAI1 at branch points remains constant relative to total dendritic staining (C117), while tip localization increases specifically at 17 DIV.

results.result: Background claims about dendritic arbor function, development, and disease relevance. These include the importance of dendritic architecture for neuronal function, its alteration in neuropsychiatric disorders including ASD, the contribution of dendrites to gray matter volume, and the limited understanding of the transition from growth to stability in hippocampal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C33 are primarily background/context claims supported by citations to established literature. These provide important context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims about dendritic function (C11, C13-C14), disease relevance (C12, C15, C21, C25-C27), and developmental mechanisms (C16-C20, C28-C33) are well-established in the field and appropriately cited. The inference that dendritic defects could contribute to brain size alterations in ASD (C24, C29) is reasonable given that dendrites comprise 30-40% of gray matter (C23), though this remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Background claims about BAI1 function and disease associations. BAI1 is an adhesion-GPCR involved in phagocytosis, angiogenesis suppression, and synaptogenesis. It is expressed in brain regions including hippocampus, and its gene is located in an ASD mutation hotspot. BAI1 SNPs associate with educational attainment, and BAI1 mRNA is elevated in mouse models of Rett and MeCP2 duplication syndromes.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C44 are background claims about BAI1 supported by citations to published literature, including the authors' previous work. These establish the rationale for studying BAI1 in the context of dendritic development and ASD. The claims about BAI1's various functions (C34, C36, C38-C40), expression patterns (C35), disease associations (C37, C41-C44), and previous mechanistic findings (C39) are well-documented in cited literature. These provide important context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background and discussion claims about RhoA function in dendrites and disease. RhoA is known to inhibit dendritic growth, but its developmental dynamics are poorly understood. The authors' findings bridge the gap between dendritic expansion during development and the requirement for RhoA inhibition for stability at later timepoints. RhoA is involved in multiple neurological diseases that exhibit altered dendritic arbors.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121, C143-C152, C156-C167 are primarily literature review and discussion claims supported by citations. The claims about RhoA's role in inhibiting dendrite growth (C120, C144-C151) are well-established but based on studies using dominant-negative/constitutively-active mutants (C145-C146), which the authors note have limitations. The claim that developmental dynamics are poorly understood (C121, C152) provides rationale for the current study. The discussion of RhoA in disease (C162-C167) and the bridging interpretation (C156) are reasonable but somewhat speculative. The pharmacological agent characterization (C157-C161) appropriately acknowledges limitations.

results.result: Discussion of differences between sparse BAI1 knockdown and global BAI1 KO, and proposed competitive advantage model. The authors propose that BAI1 confers advantages to synapses and disadvantages to dendrites that express it, explaining why sparse manipulations show strong effects while global KO shows minimal effects. This is analogous to the situation with Neuroligin-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C129-C136 address an important discrepancy between the current findings and published BAI1 KO data. The proposed competitive advantage model (C133, C136) is speculative but provides a plausible explanation for the discrepancy, supported by analogy to NL1 (C134). However, this remains a hypothesis that would require additional experiments to test directly. The characterization of the BAI1 KO phenotype (C129-C132) is based on citation to published work. The model is intellectually satisfying but lacks direct experimental support in the current manuscript.

results.result: Discussion claims about Bcr function, BAI1 signaling complexity, and therapeutic implications. Bcr possesses both Rac1-GAP and RhoA-GEF domains, with the GEF activity being cryptic. BAI1 signals through at least five mechanisms and may act as a signaling integrator. The authors speculate about ligand combinations determining downstream outcomes, therapeutic potential for correcting dendritic hypertrophy/hypotrophy in ASD, and whether dendrite retraction in neurodegeneration involves hyperactivation of restriction mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C140, C168-C186 are primarily discussion and speculation. The characterization of Bcr's dual GAP/GEF activities (C137-C140) is supported by citations. The claims about BAI1 signaling complexity (C169-C176) integrate current findings with previous work but remain somewhat speculative regarding the signaling integrator model (C176). The ligand code hypothesis (C177) is speculative but plausible given BAI1's multiple ligand-binding domains (C178). The therapeutic speculations (C168, C184-C186) are reasonable directions for future work but lack experimental support. The claim about BAI1 levels increasing during growth arrest (C181) is supported by Western blot data but is descriptive rather than mechanistic.

results.result: The results strongly implicate a BAI1-Bcr-RhoA pathway in regulating dendritic volume in the hippocampus, which is intriguing given links between BAI1 and ASD.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is a summary conclusion that is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript: (1) BAI1 loss causes dendritic overgrowth; (2) BAI1 is required for late RhoA activation; (3) RhoA activation correlates with dendrite behavior; (4) BAI1 interacts with Bcr late in development; (5) Bcr rescues BAI1 Kd phenotype; (6) Both Bcr GAP and GEF activities are required. The pathway model is strongly supported, though the specific relevance to ASD remains somewhat speculative pending additional disease-relevant experiments.
